comment: My 10 year old child was a victim of an online public information search company where my child's name and address was publically available on the web (WhitePages.com, Spokeo.com, etc.). More data on my child could be bought for a price $1 - $20. I was shocked as to how this may have happened and had to go to great lengths to have the Personally Identifiable Information removed from many similar websites. This took a lot of time and cost me in lost work hours. Many parents would not have the luxury, time, or knowledge on how to remove this data, nor should we expect them to. The Public has no time to monitor every aspect of their personal data, we expect the government to protect us from corporate abuse of our privacy. The American Public expects that PII of a minor child could never be revealed publically online or bought for a price in the first place. How was the data available? Why could someone buy/sell more information about my child? Through a children's magazine subscription that was "sold" to a paying partner? Through school? Through a Dr's office? Through apps? Corporations and computer programmers will cry that they "need" the data for their livelihood to "make thing better" for us but what about our privacy? The buying and selling of Personally Identifiable Information is shared with so many companies it makes it hard to know who to punish. I think I speak for most families when I say I do not have the time or law education to fully understand this bill but to have had this experience tells me the COPPR is not working for the online privacy of children. Please protect our children from these companies who profit from our children's data. The European Union has very strict rules concerning children, perhaps we can learn about what is working for them in this area because it's does not working for us in the United States. We cannot expect corporations to monitor themselves considering so much money can be made by selling children's data. Thank you.

The refusal of the banks' and CRAs to actually "investigate" the the obvios fraud items on my report after they had actually supplied info to the FBI for the prosecution in my case, caused me to be rejected for 2 mortages and put me through years of frustration. I have already forced one CRA to agree on demands regarding the responding to and the cleaning up of identity theft attacks and the devastating fraudulent information it leaves on consumers' credit reports. I have also succeded in creating a neew category of consumer called a "Medically incapacitated Consumer" which should be considered when establishing new industry guidelines for responding to an identity theft victim. comment: The concerns for Loot Boxes should be looking toward Gambling and the components that make up its psychological profile and effects to establish relevancy vs deviation between the two things, especially as it relates to children, adolescents, and development. I do believe there are psychological reasons why gambling is illegal for minors, not only because of their general lack of overall wealth and the increased likelihood for undue risks but because of the potential for addiction that it has? But other people would be better to highlight those facets and I hope the FTC looks into those issues seriously. Likewise, the difference between a digital-only, non-tradeable good should be considered versus the physical, resellable good of a physical good (i.e., a baseball card, a toy). Games Terms of Service explicitly disallow selling of in-game goods and services (leveling up your character for you, trading an in-game item for real world money/etc), and have and will continue to shut down people's accounts, and lock them out of service or ever participating in that game, when caught. However, in the same environment, it is not illegal to take your baseball card and sell it to another person, even if the creator company of that baseball card doesn't want you to. They have no recourse (legal or otherwise) to stop you from doing that, because it is "your" property. But in the digital space, the creator of the game has absolute say; if they say you can't trade this rare item you just found for someone else's real-world (or even in-game!) money, and ban you for it, you have no consumer protection, nor any legal opportunity to fight that undue punishment as a consumer. Likewise, when it comes to gambling, I suggest you look toward other countries: China now forces games with loot boxes (like Overwatch, a game by blizzard entertainment) to disclose percentage chances for items and objects of specific rarities (common is the most likely type of item you will get, followed by 'rare' quality, followed by mythic quality, with legendary quality being the most rare). Allowing (and keeping) the consumer aware of their chances to obtain items by quality allows them to decided with a more informed opinion on whether they do or don't want to spend money to try and acquire specific items from specific qualities, and should be a bare minimum for every single game.

comment: July 30, 2019 As the medical director of a hospitalist program at the intersection of rural Tennessee and Virginia, I have a unique perspective on the devastation caused by the opioid and addiction crises in this country, as well as the obstacles to effective solutions. While the resulting devastation of lives, families and businesses knows no socioeconomic or geographic boundaries, there are disproportionate barriers that people in rural communities face when it comes to addiction treatment. Ballad Health is partnering with East Tennessee State University (ETSU), Milligan College, Emory & Henry College and other community partners to remove these barriers. After last years merger between Wellmont and Mountain States, ETSU was able to partner with Ballad Health to create a new fellowship program in addiction medicine. Hospitals are uniquely positioned to play a critical role in stemming the tide of opioid addiction, but the effort requires more highly trained and certified providers available at these reachable moments in the care path. As part of its commitment to expand education and training in the region, the newly-merged Ballad Health is set to fund any un-reimbursed costs of this fellowship program, which over a 10-year period could top more than $2.5 million. In May of this year, Milligan College announced its own partnership with Ballad Health to create a training program in addictions counseling, helping to round out education for the continuum of care in addiction treatment by adding a pipeline of counseling professionals to complement the medical professionals coming through the ETSU program. Ballad Health is also working to strengthen the pipeline of medical professionals who can help extend the reach of physician in primary care and other settings. I have personally participated in training for physician assistants through the Emory & Henry College School of Health Sciences, and their students perform rotations in our Virginia facilities. In addition to these training programs, of note is Ballad Healths $85 million investment commitment in behavioral health, which is helping to strengthen addiction recovery services and community partnerships like Overmountain Recovery. In a region that is among both the top 10 nationally for opioid abuse AND second in the nation for rural hospital closures over the past decade, these types of investments are urgent. The fact that those investments are being made is cause for optimism. Nothing short of innovative and locally-focused public, private and academic partnerships will be able to halt the trajectory of this regions addiction crisis. The programs at ETSU and Milligan College would not have gotten off the ground without the commitment and combined resources from Ballad Health, of which I remain a strong supporter. Regards, Shyam Odeti, MD, MS, FAAFP, FHM.

comment: COPA legislation is simply a mechanism for large hospitals to engage in monopolistic activities free from FTC oversight in clear violation of consumer protection laws. Hospitals wishing to illegally merge often employ lobbyists that work to convince part-time state legislators of the merits of such legislation. These efforts are well funded and can rarely be opposed by the smaller businesses they will ultimately harm or consumers that will be negatively impacted as a result of the monopolies that COPA allows. Most state legislators have very little understanding of the nuances of healthcare insurance and reimbursement and can be easily cajoled into supporting COPA legislation when it is presented under the banner of well-known supposedly not-for-profit hospitals and seemingly admirable goals such as eliminating waste, clinical integration or saving a struggling hospital. Economic studies regarding the impact of hospital consolidations are unequivocal in their condemnation of the negative impact these mergers have on pricing, quality, new competition and consumer choice. COPA legislation is extremely difficult to enforce post-merger even if states have the resources to do so, which they do not. The impact that mergers have on the marketplace often takes years to be fully realized. By the time their impact is apparent to consumers and enforcement agencies, there is very little that enforcement can do to truly "put the cat back in the bag". Certain aspects of the ACA have made hospital consolidation more likely and consumer protection more difficult. The FTC should clearly define it's position with respect to certain provisions of the ACA that tend to inspire hospital mergers. The FTC should aggressively seek to limit the state's ability to circumvent consumer protection laws through strong federal enforcement. The FTC should study and publish definitive empirical market data regarding not just COPA... but also hospital consolidations more broadly. The FTC should proactively and vigorously oppose COPA legislation at the state level. The FTC should address the growing issue of hospital prices and their impact on mergers with independent physicians, competition and consumer pricing. The FTC should study the impact hospital mergers have on "quality" through a framework of measurable standard outcomes.

comment: As a practicing pediatric ophthalmologist in an academic environment, I am very concerned about proposals included in the Federal Trade Commission's proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule. We always prioritize patient safety, but the prescription-receipt verification process and three-year record hold places an unfair burden on ophthalmology practices. This new burden is also unwarranted, as there is little evidence that ophthalmologists are not in compliance with the existing Contact Lens Rule. Such an administrative burden should not be placed on any business that is already going to great lengths to comply with the Contact Lens Rule and do so despite serious concerns with the current prescription-verification system that we believe puts our patients at risk. I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw its latest proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule and focus on efforts to enhance patient safety. Thank you for your consideration.

comment: I am a manager in a high-tech, US-based, secure computer design and manufacturing firm. We have run into significant problems from certain component vendors that overlap with right to repair legislation. Specifically, certain vendors require all firmware components to be signed with their vendor key in order for the firmware to execute. This severely impairs the repair capability of their devices, increases e-waste when the vendor is unwilling to fix known bugs in their firmware (recommending for instance to buy a newer or more expensive device and discard the old one) and also severely limits innovation in fields that the vendor has not considered. When the vendor is the only manufacturer creating a specific class of computing peripheral, this has the effect of not only stifling repair of entire classes of devices, but also encouraging foreign (usually Asian) companies to innovate where US citizens and corporations are locked out by vendor decisions. Any right to repair guidelines in today's high tech, firmware-driven world must address the issue of vendor cryptographic signatures being required to replace existing malfunctioning firmware on hardware devices. Ideally this would take the form of an alternate operating mode being required that does not check the firmware signature, but also indicates the device is operating outside of the vendor controlled mode. This would allow e.g. DRM systems to function on the vendor firmware, but still allow owner repair / replacement of firmware with deactivation of the DRM systems (i.e. inability to decrypt protected content using unsigned firmware, but the ability to repair the rest of the device functionality). We have already seen significant damage in the overall economy, ranging from impacts caused by the signed Intel ME/ AMD PSP along with, for example, NVIDIA's cryptographic signing forcing continual replacement of otherwise functional cards. This requirement to replace and discard is usually due to firmware or firmware-enforced driver bugs that NVIDIA is unwilling to fix for commercial reasons. Please take action and put a stop to this, allow American companies to innovate again, reduce our e-waste, and restore the right to repair complex firmware-driven systems.

comment: Ballad Health can and has begun its process of removing neonatal care from HVMC. The current contract for neonatologists expires August 31st. After that, it is unclear exactly what their plans are to ensure babies who are born prematurely, drug exposed, or full-term with unexpected medical needs receive the care they require. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, VLBW infants (those born 2 weighing 3.3 pounds or less) born at non-level III care who were stabilized and then transported had a 62% increase in odds of neonatal or pre-discharge mortality compared with those born at level III hospitals (as we currently have). Last year, Holston Valley Medical Center had almost 100 babies born prematurely that fit into this category. So, with the decision to eliminate the HVMC NICU, is the intentional decision to increase the mortality rate of almost 100 babies in our region by 62% unnecessarily. In addition, our NICU had 83 babies in 2018 born drug-exposed and 96 full-term babies that required Level III NICU care. MY GRANDSON, was born in 2017 and weighed a little over 11lbs! Had it of not been for the NICU.....there is a possibility he would have had severe complications. The cost to run Holston Valleys NICU as a Level III facility is approximately $1.5 Million per year. The cost to run a Level I well-baby nursery as they plan is $500,000 saving them $1 Million per year. Ballad Health announced a $66 Million Net Income increase for the fiscal quarter. That money could run our NICU as a Level III facility for 66 years alone. So, tell me why were jeopardizing the lives of approximately 300 babies again?????? ***NOTE: The Holston Valley Neonatologists provide support for approximately 1700 babies born in our region every year. LEVEL 1 TRAUMA CENTER: In preparation for the consolidation of Level I Trauma services, the hospital administration gathered the data for comparison between Holston Valley Medical Center and Johnson City Medical Center. The data was to demonstrate the value of Holston Valley Medical Center as a Level I Trauma Center. Bishop & Associates was to use the data in their determination of which location to retain Level I Trauma Services at after the merger. It is not known if this material was provided to Bishop & Associates; only that hospital administration acquired this data and it was to be shared with them for their consultation. Per Ballad Health, Bishop & Associates determined that Johnson City Medical Center was the best location to retain the Level I Trauma services. 23 Counties in Northeast Tennessee and Southwest Virginia were compared to determine the best location to retain Level I Trauma services based on driving time. With trauma, the first 60 minutes are critical to survival. Referred to as the golden hour, these 60 minutes are often the determining factor in a patients outcome. In this data, the drive times are compared and assigned a weighted score. (The lower the number the better.) Only 8 of 23 Counties are within 60 Minute Drive Time to Johnson City Medical Center. 11 of 23 Counties are within 60 Minutes Drive Time to Holston Valley Medical Center. Weighted Scores (the lower the better): Holston Valley Medical Center: 542.22 Johnson City Medical Center: 585.10 As demonstrated by the numbers, Holston Valley is more accessible to the majority of the service region in receiving life-saving Level I Trauma Care within the critical golden hour - 60 minutes. This data is the most disturbing as it effectively demonstrates the conscious choice by Ballad Health to choose the facility where the least amount of people can get access to Level I Trauma care when they live exactly 60 minutes from the facility. These numbers do not include the population that lives more than or less than 60 minutes drive time from the facility, but rather ONLY 60 minutes. 12 out of 23 counties had a portion of their population exactly 60 minutes from Holston Valley Medical Center totaling 84,147 people. 6 out of 23 counties had a portion of their population exactly 60 minutes from Johnson City Medical Center totaling 17,750 people. By choosing Johnson City Medical Center as the location for the Level I Trauma services, Ballad Health Administration knowingly and intentionally chose to exclude 84,147 people from accessing Level I Trauma care within the critical, life-saving 60 minutes (golden hour). The data is conclusive and alarming given Ballad Healths decision to downgrade Holston Valley Medical Center to a Level III Trauma Center and retain Johnson City Medical as the only Level I Trauma Center in a region servicing 29 counties and 1.2 million people. DISCLAIMER: This is a personal interpretation of the data. I am not employed by nor do I represent Ballad Health, Bishop & Associates, or any other organization. I am a private citizen advocating for access to quality healthcare.

Attachment 1_ PTW Report to FTC.pdf Attachment 2_ Spread Sheet Rolex Parts.xisx ABSTRACT This report presents a research study concerning pricing effects on restricted Rolex watch parts based on 2008 wholesale prices compared to that of 2019. Data is presented in spreadsheet form and demonstrates that the open market average wholesale price increased by 563% over that period compared to a 19% inflation rate. It is shown that this is a consequence of restricted parts policies of the manufacturer and is discussed in the context of a gray versus black market for goods.
